title: The Distracted Classroom
bodyMarkdown: Midway through a lecture you notice a cluster of students in the back row have stopped taking notes and are quietly talking among themselves. The rest of the class is still following along. You have about twenty minutes of material left to cover before the period ends. What do you do in the moment, and what, if anything, would you change about the rest of the session?

title: The Silent Question
bodyMarkdown: After explaining a concept you consider straightforward, you ask if there are any questions. Nobody responds, but a few faces suggest confusion rather than understanding. You are on a tight schedule and the next topic builds directly on this one. How do you find out what's actually unclear, and how does your answer change if this happens in a class of 40 versus a class of 400?

title: The Uneven Group
bodyMarkdown: You've assigned a group project, and it's now clear that one student in each group is doing most of the work while the others coast. Grades are due at the end of the term and are meant to reflect individual contribution, but you only have the group's final submission and your own occasional observations to go on. How do you assess this fairly, and what would you do differently the next time you assign group work?

title: The Buffet
bodyMarkdown:
Most of us divide the assignment marks in one of a few ways. One assignment for twenty marks. Or two of ten. Or four of five. The speaker's objection is a simple one: in none of these does the student get a choice.

So the speaker does it differently. Five or six assignments go on the table, of different sizes and different depths. One at four or six marks, kept deliberately easy, for the student who is struggling to get through the course. One at ten. One that is open-ended, worth fifteen or sixteen, cutting across units, for the student the talk calls knowledge-hungry. Students then pick any combination they like until they reach twenty marks.

The speaker calls it a buffet. Each student takes what suits their appetite. Having chosen, they own whatever that assignment demands. And because two students chose different assignments, they are evaluated differently. There is no comparison between them.

The speaker is honest about what this costs the teacher. Do it in one of your three courses, the advice runs, not in all three. Begin with two or three options, not six. Every assignment you offer is an assignment you will have to evaluate, and a teacher who is worn down by that load teaches all three courses worse.

Now place it in your own semester. Six assignments mean six rubrics. Seventy students choosing freely means you are evaluating five different kinds of work in the same fortnight, not one. Within three days of the list going up, the class group has worked out which combination gives the most marks for the least effort. That is what most of the plates will look like. The course file asks you to map every assignment to a course outcome, and the four-mark revision assignment does not map where the sixteen-mark one does. At the end, the mark sheet shows one number out of twenty. It does not show which route the student took. Two students holding eighteen have done work of very different sizes, and the placement filter reading that column cannot see the difference. Inside your course, there is no comparison between them. The moment that number leaves your course, the comparison is the only thing left.

Both answers cost something. Leave the choice completely open, and a student can reach the full twenty marks four at a time, taking only the easiest assignments on the table. They will not have broken a single rule. The design that respects the student's choice is the same design that lets them choose never to be stretched. Make one assignment from the deep end compulsory, and you have taken back the thing that made it work. The student is no longer choosing. They are completing a requirement with a menu attached, and the ownership the whole design was for goes with it.

Now suppose you had put the buffet on the table. It is week six, and one student's plate reads four marks, four marks, four marks. You do not know which student you are looking at. It may be someone spreading thin effort across five courses in a bad semester. It may be someone who has done the arithmetic and decided that sixteen marks is not worth what the open-ended assignment will cost. Or it may be someone who has never once been asked to work at that depth, and does not believe they can. What would tell you which of the three it is? And once you know, does it change what you do, or only how you feel about doing it?
